Basecamp's ONCE Campfire · the F# port, unchained

onCrack.

The same Campfire, pixel for pixel, on a server that is free to do less work: it keeps finished pages until a commit changes what they show, and commits concurrent posts together. Who may see a kept page is decided again on every request, as upstream asks. Two claims, each with its evidence one click away. Every number on this page links to the file it came from.

Claim one

Faster.

Ahead of current upstream Rust and C at the median in every workload of Basecamp's own harness, with the room being written to and without. Quote the range, not one number: the three sessions of each profile, pooled, read as below; each session on its own reads 2.11× to 4.74× over Rust (normal) and 3.00× to 6.33× (mixed), because 4 of the 6 sessions ran beside other projects' work.

  • 3.76×over Rust f9dca47
  • 2.40×over C cd0cbe4
  • 5.25×over the F# port
  • Fresh authorization. The default re-checks the session and the room membership on every cache hit, as upstream's contract asks. The cached decision, opt-in, reads 4.19× over Rust.
  • Per room page, the CPU says the same: Rust spends 3.79× and C 2.93× of onCrack's CPU (3.75× and 2.68× on the quiet host).
  • Mixed reads: 3.76× over Rust and 2.26× over C while one writer posts into the room.

The evidence →Not their machine: four of a VM's CPUs a side. Compare ratios.

Claim two

More runnable in production.

Fast is easy to buy by dropping what production needs. onCrack keeps the pixels, the durability and every connected client, and it says what that costs.

  • 0of 1,000 Cable clients cut in PR #6's heaviest profile, in 3 of 3 rounds. Rust cut 902 to 959 of them.
  • 944/944screenshots pixel-equal to Rails, on every seed, on the final code.
  • 13,571/13,571posted messages reached every client in the median round, and every posted message did in every round. Rust: 65 of 76,602.
  • Durability is Rails'. Every write commits before it is answered; nothing weaker ships. The last kill -9 runs (4 of them, round three) lost 0 and duplicated 0.
  • Cable's backlog is bounded. A shared log with a byte budget, 1 GiB for the whole hub; over it, the clients furthest behind are cut. Its known slack is in the report.
  • It holds the posters, not the readers. It takes 902 posts a second to Rust's 5,102, a 9 s p99 from a post to the slowest client, and about 996 MB of memory to Rust's 125. A different policy, not a free win.

  2. Port, the tuning 6 Oct – 7 Oct

    Match Rust's profile.

    Parity first, then tuning against Rust's own profile: cookies, bodies, row reads, Cable fan-out. Published as the F# port; onCrack forks from its last dot.

    Closing headline. Final re-baseline: 1.24–1.33× Rust at 16 connections.

    On the chart at its close: the port 1.32×.

  3. Round one 7 Oct – 8 Oct

    Keep finished pages.

    Same pixels, unhinged work per request: a versioned read cache, group commit, Content-Length on gzipped answers, Native AOT as an opt-in.

    Closing headline. 3.84× Rust and 2.89× the port at 16 connections: a result in which every read was a cache hit.

    On the chart at its close: cached 3.82×.

  4. Round two 8 Oct – 9 Oct

    Make the benchmark honest, then go faster.

    A benchmark that writes while it reads, Cable on its own socket, a front-server fast path, memory and cold start. It ended against upstream's own harness.

    Closing headline. 3.25× Rust, 2.37× C and 3.93× the port on upstream's harness, with the cached decision, which is not upstream's contract.

    On the chart at its close: cached 4.98×.

  5. Round three 9 Oct

    Check who is asking, every time.

    Fresh authorization on every cache hit became the default (R3.2), search by message id as upstream's (R3.3). The cached decision stays an opt-in.

    Closing headline. Fresh: 2.59× Rust, 1.86× C, 3.82× the port on upstream's harness (two sessions pooled: 2.68× and 3.33× on their own).

    On the chart, its final image measured in round five: fresh 4.32×, cached 4.64×.

  6. Round four

    Fan-out, and keep every subscriber.

    Gather writes (one sendmsg over the frames) and Cable reliability: a shared byte-bounded log, a cut for a stall and not for slowness, a gate that slows the posters. The fan-out lead at the largest room was withdrawn.

    Closing headline. 3.29× Rust, 2.40× C on one session; fan-out 1.59×, 1.24×, 1.16× and 0.94× Rust at 100, 500, 1,000 and 2,000 clients.

    No dot: nothing was logged on this suite in round four.

  7. Round five 13 Oct

    Find the one message.

    The one message that did not arrive was a compiler turning a recursion into a loop in the gather's pinning: found by reading the IL, fixed, tested. The memory bound now covers every chunk. Then the final gates and runs.

    Closing headline. 3.76× Rust, 2.40× C, 5.25× the port on upstream's harness, across sessions of 2.11× to 4.74×; no client cut in PR #6.

    On the chart at its close: fresh 4.63×, cached 4.90×.

The honest version · round one, pinned Rust ccece30

Cache hits, and the other end.

A stored page is only as good as the writes that don't touch it. So the same room page was read at 16 connections while one more connection posted into that very room as fast as each app would take it: about 1,100 posts a second, each one invalidating the page.

Room page reads a second at 16 connections, same scale in both. How it was measured →

What onCrack does that Rust and the port don't

Less work per request.

The HTML is byte for byte the port's and Rust's. What changed is how often it gets made, and how it goes out. Each idea states the rule that keeps it correct.

Versioned read cache

A trigger bumps a counter inside the write's own transaction. A stored page is served only while every counter it was built under is unchanged.

Group commit

Posts that arrive together share one transaction, a savepoint each, one commit. Every post is committed before it is answered.

One send, not two

A cached gzip page goes out with its Content-Length instead of chunked, so it no longer needs a second send to end it.

Native AOT, opt-in

Starts in 98 ms instead of 218, but serves less at 16 connections, so the default stays JIT.

The four, with their rules and their numbers →

Fan-out

One message, a thousand clients.

A post goes out over Action Cable to everyone in the room. onCrack delivers 1.65× Rust's messages a second at 100 clients, 1.24× at 500 and 1.17× at 1,000: ahead, with every rep of onCrack above every rep of Rust in the one quiet session of the three. At 2,000 clients it is 1.01×, level, not ahead: the reps overlap and both servers are bound by the sendmsg syscall. Every message reached every client in every one of the 140 Cable phases of the final run.

Reads while writing

The honest read/write mix

×

bench/run's read workloads ask for one URL over and over and never write, so onCrack answers every request from a stored page. The table on the main page (4.34× Rust on the room page) is that best case. This is the other end.

How

review/mixed.sh: 16 connections read the room page while one connection posts into the same room as fast as the app answers. Every post moves the room's counter, so every post throws the stored page away. 30 s together as a warm-up, then a measured window; two runs per app, in opposite orders (6 runs in all).

What onCrack does that Rust and the port don't

Four changes, four rules

×

Four changes, measured one at a time against the build without them. The HTML a browser gets is unchanged (its decoded bytes equal Rust's on every probed route), and each change has a switch that turns it off.

The versioned read cache

A global counter, one per room, one per user and one for sessions. Triggers bump them inside the write's transaction. Room counters are striped: ids equal modulo 65,536 share one, so a URL naming rooms that don't exist can't grow memory (the verifier's finding).

The triggers (TEMP, on the writer's connection only, so the database file keeps Rails' schema)
A write toBumps
messagesits room
boosts; a message's rich text and attachmentsthe message's room (global if the message is gone)
roomsthe room; created or destroyed: the room and global
membershipsadded or removed: the room and the user; updated: the user
searches, push subscriptionsthe user
sessionssessions
accounts, users, bans, webhooks, blobs, variants, other rich textglobal
the search index (no triggers possible)the message's room, by the job that writes it
What each stored page depends on
PageDepends on
room page, messages pagethe global counter (under which its user was read), the user, the room
sidebar, searchthe global counter, the user, every room the user is in
the session (authentication)the sessions counter
the signed-in userthe global counter

The invalidation rule. The first bump of a counter in a write makes it odd, before the row changes; the write's end (after the commit and its after-commit work, before the caller hears back) makes it even, one past. A request takes its counters before its first query, keeps the page only if all were even and are unchanged when it finishes, and a stored page is served only while every counter still equals what it was kept under. So nothing is served across a committed change, and a writer always reads its own write.

Never shared across users: the key starts with the user's id, then everything the render reads from the request (route, full URL, host, Turbo-Frame, Referer, User-Agent, the last_room cookie). A request with a flash message is not cached. The store is bounded at 64 MB in two generations. CAMPFIRE_READ_CACHE=off turns it off.

Group commit

The single writer takes every write already queued (up to 64) and runs them in one transaction, a savepoint each, with one COMMIT; then the group's after-commit work in one more transaction; then the cache counters are released; then every caller is answered, in queue order. It never waits for a group to fill (the window is 0 µs), so at one connection every group is one write.

The durability rule. Every post is committed before its response is written: WAL with synchronous=normal, Rails' own setting. A write that fails rolls back to its savepoint alone; anything that breaks the group's transaction leaves nothing committed and the group runs again write by write. Broadcasts go out in commit order.

Content-Length on cached gzip answers

The port copies Rack::Deflater and sends gzip chunked, which costs a second send for the terminating chunk. For a gzipped buffer or a stored page onCrack makes the gzip member before the headers, sends its length and writes it once. Streams, files and pages rendered in parts stay chunked. CAMPFIRE_GZIP_LENGTH=off restores chunking. On a search at c=16, syscalls per request fell from 18.1 to 10.0.

Native AOT, as an opt-in

docker build --build-arg NATIVE_AOT=true makes campfire-oncrack:aot. It starts in 98 ms against the default image's 218, idles at 22 MB against 38, and passes the pixel gate (361 screenshots, the fast matrix on the default seed). But without tiered PGO it serves 0.90× of the default image at 16 connections (1.14× at one), and it loses HTTP/2 without TLS. The headline is throughput at 16 connections, so the default stays JIT + ReadyToRun.

Sources: bench/results/oncrack-c4.md, bench/results/oncrack-c4/boot.jsonl, bench/results/oncrack-c4/tier3-aot/oncrack-1.json, bench/results/oncrack-c3/tier3/oncrack-1.json.

The major bug: a stale user row

What: authentication read the signed-in user before the page took its counters. A change to that user committing in between was rendered from the old row and stored under the new counters, then served until an unrelated write moved one: the name in the room page's meta tag and composer, the sidebar's name and avatar, and the administrator-only New Chat Room button.

Found by A1, A1b and A1c, each making 1,500 changes while 12 other browsers read the page: 93 and 75 stale room pages in two runs, 50 stale sidebars, 79 sidebars showing the wrong role. With the cache off, all three found 0.

The fix and its rule: a page's global dependency is now the global counter's value the user was read under, not one taken when the action starts. A page whose user changed since is neither kept nor served; a page whose user was not read through the cache is rendered but not kept. Three tests in ReadCacheTests make 1,000 changes while 12 browsers read; before the fix each failed, after it all pass twice in a row, and also with the cache off.

The minor ones

  • A counter for every room id in a URL (A2): fixed by striping room counters modulo 65,536, at most a 512 KB array per database.
  • Group commit broadcast concurrent posts out of commit order (A5), more often than the port: fixed with a line of places taken in commit order; now all 320 posts of the test arrive with 0 out-of-order pairs, group commit on and off.
  • bin/kit-differential http failed by default because of the added Content-Length: it now accepts exactly the gzip member's length and nothing else, with a self-test.

Gates

Before the fixes the verifier also ran bin/verify, bin/db-differential, bin/kit-differential and the full pixel gate; after them bin/verify ran 1,075 tests with 0 failed. The verifier's report is kept verbatim beside its tests.

Durability

Rails' default, and nothing weaker

×

onCrack ships Rails' durability and nothing weaker. The plan allowed weaker settings only behind a switch whose default is Rails'; none was needed. Group commit shares the commit, not the durability: Rails' synchronous=normal already doesn't fsync per commit, so there was no per-post sync to share.

Default against the alternatives
SettingDefaultWhat it doesThe other way
CAMPFIRE_GROUP_COMMITonGrouped writes, a savepoint each, one commit. Every post commits before it is answered.off: one write per transaction, the port's writer
CAMPFIRE_GROUP_COMMIT_WINDOW_US0The writer never waits for a group to fill.a wait only adds latency; durability is the same
journal_mode, synchronouswal, normalRails' own settings, unchanged.nothing weaker exists to turn on
synchronous=fullnot builtStronger than Rails: an fsync per commit, which group commit could share.not built or measured

Killed mid-write

The verifier posted from 16 threads with the default settings, killed the container with SIGKILL mid-run, restarted it on the same storage and looked for every post that had been answered 200. 3 runs: 9,656 acknowledged posts, 0 lost, 0 duplicated, 0 missing from the search index, and the newest acknowledged post was on the room page after the restart. A few posts per run were stored but never acknowledged: committed, killed before the answer went out, which is the order the rule promises.

Measured both ways

A commit window costs the single connection its whole wait per post and gains nothing at 16 or 64 connections, where the queue already fills groups, so it stays at 0.

The rule onCrack works under: every parity screen's pixels must match Rails'. The server's HTML, the live DOM and Cable frames may differ; what a person sees may not.

How it was run

  • bin/pixel-parity against the Rails reference, the harness's lean matrix: every state on Chromium (desktop and phone, light and dark), the smoke states on Firefox and WebKit, and the breakpoint sweep, on all 5 seeds, on the image campfire-oncrack:app built from a clean worktree at the final commit (ee5a2e9). src/ is the code the verifier closed on: nothing in it changed after the gate.
  • This is the full gate on the final code. Round three ran the full gate on its own final code (940 screenshots); the 4 more here are Chromium cells of search/results/order, the state round three added after that gate to tell the two search orders apart.
  • The default seed ran in twelve slices so each fit one call; the slices partition its states, and pixel_parity.py checks that no cell ran in two of them. A cell counts by its last attempt that captured it, as bin/pixel-parity counts it. The room page capture is byte-identical on both sides and equals round one's.

Three harness faults, none a pixel difference

  • auth/sign_in/error was not captured in three attempts (the harness waits 30 s for stylesheets on a freshly started server, as in rounds one and three); a fourth run of that state alone captured all four cells, all equal.
  • The harness crashed 50 cells into realtime/** (Response has been disposed, an unhandled rejection in its network capture), and one re-run sat for 40 minutes with the VM idle; both passed when run again in smaller slices with a watchdog.
  • No clean first-pass gate was obtained, and the Mac's 12 GiB free-space floor was breached several times by another project's Go build cache; the results file says so in full. Nothing in src/ or the harness was changed for any of it.

The reports themselves (every screenshot and diff) are gitignored under parity/out/pixel-parity-r5-final/; pixel_parity.py keeps what they say. The page's build reads its pixel-parity.json.

Is the load generator the limit?

A fast server can be under-measured by a slow client. The load generator runs on its own 4 cores, and the session recorded how busy they were in every window.

  • At onCrack's fastest workload cell the load generator used 3.04 of its 4 cores, leaving 1.0 idle, while the server used 3.76 of its 4: the server is the one at its limit.
  • The rig went faster in the same session: the same load generator drove 217,948 requests a second at the CSS file (onCrack, 64 connections), 1.41× onCrack's fastest workload cell. So the workload numbers are not the rig's ceiling.
  • The host stayed quiet: after each of the 288 measured windows a probe timed a fixed spin on the pinned CPUs; the worst was 1.08× its baseline.
  • Not measured: a second load generator, or a client on another machine. The VM has 8 CPUs, split evenly, so neither side can be given more without taking from the other.

The post path costs more CPU than it did. On this project's own suite a post cost 188.4 µs of server CPU in round three's final image and 213.8 in the final one (fresh, 1.13× over). Where Rust is faster, and where it ties

At 2,000 clients the two are level on throughput and both are bound by the sendmsg syscall, which took three quarters of the server's CPU in the profile; no default changed, because the one setting that helped there cost the smaller sizes. Rust is clearly faster in paced latency at 100 clients (3.3 against 5.2 ms, 1.55×), and its memory is under half of onCrack's at every size (onCrack's saturated Pss is 2.70× to 2.77× of Rust's).

Every message arrived

In every Cable phase of the three sessions (140 phases: three apps, four sizes, saturated and paced, the sends passes included) every posted message reached every client, nobody was closed mid-run, and no frame was odd. Round four had one phase in which a message of 34,741 did not reach every client; its cause was the server (a payload moved under the kernel by a collection, because the gather pinned only the last payload of a batch), it was fixed with a test that fails on the old code, and it has not recurred in 105 target phases since. 0 phases flagged by the rule of cable/phases.py, which this page's build runs on every build and refuses to publish if it flags one.

Three sessions were run; only the quiet one is the headline

oneComplete except Rust's third rep (the harness read a memory file at the instant the sampler renamed it); not pooled, re-run66
twoAll reps complete; the sends pass stopped by the disk guard and finished in a continuation; not pooled, re-run64
threeAll parts, one uninterrupted session: the headline7

How the picture is drawn

Each lane sends pulses from its hub at a rate in proportion to its measured messages a second; at a given N one pulse stands for the same number of messages in every lane, and each dot for ten clients. The pulses are CSS animations, so they run without JavaScript; with JavaScript each lane also counts what it has delivered since you opened the page, and how far behind Rust that leaves it. With reduced motion nothing moves and the rates are what you read.

A difference of policy, not a free win

Action Cable never cuts a client for being slow: whatever the socket will not take waits in a queue of that connection's own, with no bound, which is what Rails' memory above is; its posters are slow enough that the queues stay short. Rust and onCrack before the shared log post far faster than they can send to a thousand clients, ran past a ring of a few hundred frames, and closed the clients that fell behind: the harness counts them as disconnected and they miss everything after. onCrack now keeps what the slowest client has not read once, in a log its clients share, cuts a client only when the log it pins passes a byte budget or its socket takes no byte for half a minute, and makes a post wait (at most two seconds) while most of a room is seconds behind. So it takes fewer posts than the cutting servers do, and delivers every one of them to every client. A browser that is cut reconnects and fetches what it missed.

Two policies for a reader that cannot keep up: cut it, or slow the posters (the harness's own posts-a-second count, each round)

The F# port cannot take the overload profile, so only its Cable profiles ran: its contract preparation stops at the search order (the port keeps Rails' order; upstream's contract wants message id order). In its cable_heavy rounds it closed clients in two of the three and ended with posts undelivered.

Read with care

  • C's Cable server did not take most of the clients in this setup, in either profile (its subscribed count is well under the 1,000), so its row says only that: its disconnected count also counts clients closed while still connecting, and it says nothing about cutting slow clients. Not investigated.
  • One disturbance. The Mac's disk guard stopped the session's wrapper once, in Rust's second overload round, and not the harness, which ran on; nothing was dropped or re-run, and the wrapper now stops the harness too (the results file has the minute-by-minute).
  • The host was not noisy for this session (under the plan's line), unlike round four's, which was stopped half-way.

The commands

The final run

Everything below the page's headline ran from this plan, with every session's host load sampled every ten seconds and each session's noise judged by a rule written before it. Run from the repository root on branch crack, inside the colima VM where the harness needs Linux.

# the final run (round five), plan fixed first: bench/results/oncrack-r5-final/PLAN.md
CAMPFIRE_REVISION=$(git rev-parse HEAD) parity/bin/candidate build        # in the clean measured worktree, then bin/clean-docker and bin/clean-parity
colima ssh -- bash -c "$PWD/bench/results/oncrack-r5-final/scripts/pixel-gate.sh"   # the full gate, every seed; then:
python3 bench/results/oncrack-r5-final/pixels/pixel_parity.py
CAMPFIRE_REQUIRE_SEED=1 bin/verify; bin/linux-tests Cable
bench/run --apps rust,fsharp,oncrack --suites cable --clients 100 500 1000 2000 --reps 3
bin/benchmark --rounds 3 --duration 8 --concurrencies 16 --cpus 0-3 --client-cpus 4-7 \
  --apps rails,rust,c,fsharp,oncrack,oncrack-cached --routes room_show,messages_page,sidebar,search,post_message   # mixed: four reads and --mixed-write-rate 10

Round one's commands

Everything runs inside the colima VM (colima ssh -- bash -c "cd $PWD && ..."), from the repository root, on branch crack. Each app's rep runs in parts, one container per part, merged into the rep's file, so every part fits one call. Order: Rails, Rust, the port, onCrack in reps one and three, reversed in rep two.

CAMPFIRE_REVISION=$(git rev-parse HEAD) parity/bin/candidate build     # then bin/clean-docker from macOS
R=bench/results/oncrack-round1-final/review
$R/quiet.sh && $R/part.sh reference 1 'room_show messages_page'   # ... sidebar search | avatar static_css up | post_message
$R/quiet.sh && $R/part.sh oncrack 1 'post_message' 'http cable upload'   # each rep's last part
bench/report bench/results/oncrack-round1-final > bench/results/oncrack-round1-final/report.md
python3 bench/results/oncrack-round1-final/review/table.py
$R/manual.sh rust; $R/manual.sh oncrack; $R/mixed.sh rust|fsharp|oncrack; $R/bytes.sh
bin/pixel-parity --seeds crowd,custom_styles,first_run,restricted
bin/pixel-parity --seeds default --only 'realtime/**'   # ... twelve slices (SLICES in pixel_parity.py)
python3 bench/results/oncrack-r3-pixels/pixel_parity.py
python3 site/same_pixels.py && python3 site/build.py

Fixed

  • Seed: parity/.seed/default, copied fresh for every run; signed in as David.
  • CPU pinning: the server on CPUs 0-3, the load generator on 4-7, host networking (SERVER_CPUS, LOADGEN_CPUS).
  • Schedule: apps reference,rust,fsharp,oncrack, reps 3; suites: http; http secs 8, concs 1 16 64, routes room_show messages_page, warm-up 30s at each route and concentration, idle 10s.
  • Warm-up: every route at its measured concurrency until flat (bench/lib/warmup.py); the VM's load waited down before every part (review/quiet.sh).
  • Durability: the defaults. No setting that weakens it was used.

Evidence for claim one

Fresh authorization, against Rust, C and the port

×

Upstream's contract re-reads the session and the room membership on every cache hit; until round three onCrack kept the decision its first request made and dropped it on any commit. Now, by default, every request reads its session and user rows, a kept room or messages page is served after a membership query finds the row, and the front server's replay first runs one narrow query for the session, its user and the membership. A room page hit costs 1.05× the CPU of the cached decision on a quiet host: CAMPFIRE_FRESH_AUTH=0 keeps the cached decision as an opt-in.

The plan, fixed before any session ran, pools every round of every session of a profile and drops none. It re-runs a session once when more than a quarter of its host samples show other work at a core and a half or more. 4 of the 6 sessions were over that line (other projects' Erlang VMs, Go test binaries and Python workers on the same Mac), so the pooled figure carries them, and each profile spent its whole budget of three sessions. The noise is not symmetric: onCrack's reads need about two and a half of the four client cores for a hundred and sixty thousand requests a second, so other work on those cores lowers them more than it lowers Rust's or C's, and its post path (the disk) fell tenfold under another project's fsyncs. The first two sessions of each profile, the design the plan started from, read 3.19× over Rust and 2.44× over C (normal), 3.96× and 2.15× (mixed): inside the range, not a different answer. Quote the range, and the CPU per request, which is the steadier number.

Read with care

  • No quiet repeat of the headline. The two sessions that passed the noise rule read 2.11× and 6.33× over Rust (normal and mixed), so a quiet host did not make the figure steadier here. A reading nobody can dispute needs a Mac with nothing else on it.
  • The fresh-over-cached ratio is not a result. The two share an image and differ by one lookup; in the pooled tables they read 0.90× and 0.83×, in the hand re-runs level (1.03× on a room page). The cells swing several-fold inside a session.
  • Not their machine. Four of this VM's CPUs per side, not the Ryzen's; compare ratios, not absolute numbers, with their report. Rust and C are upstream's own images.
  • One normal session was set aside whole (it ran the harness's default eight routes by mistake): kept in full beside the others, not pooled; it shows onCrack ahead on the three extra routes too.

Read with care

  • Not their machine. Four of this VM's CPUs per side, not the Ryzen's; compare ratios, not absolute numbers, with their report.
  • A different freshness mechanism, then. Upstream re-reads the session and membership on every cache hit. In round two onCrack kept the decision and dropped it on any commit, by any connection (it watches SQLite's WAL index); the round's verifier attacked that with foreign writers and it held, but a hit was not the same work as theirs. Round three made fresh authorization the default; its numbers are the headline.
  • Search order. Rails 90b3300 lists a search's matches by time; upstream has listed them by message id since dbc7620. onCrack now lists them by id and passes upstream's contract unchanged. The port still renders the old order, so the harness checks it against that one.
  • One viewer, one URL. Their read workloads are a cache-hit benchmark; the appendix of the results file keeps this project's realistic workloads.

Evidence for claim two

What “runnable in production” stands on

×

“Runnable in production” is eight checks and one price. Each is a number from the final run, and where to read it.

What the claim stands on
CheckResultMore
Nobody is cutonCrack at HEAD, fresh and cached: 0 of 1,000 clients disconnected in every one of the 3 rounds of PR #6's cable_heavy and cable profiles. Rust cut 902 to 959 in cable_heavy; onCrack before the shared log, 833 to 860.The tables
Every message arrivesIn the median round of cable_heavy all 13,571 posted messages reached every client, and in every one of the 12 cable and cable_heavy runs of onCrack, fresh and cached, every posted message did. In the Cable suite, 140 phases of three sessions: none short of any client, none closed, no odd frame.The fan-out
The same pixels944 of 944 screenshots pixel-equal to Rails on every seed, on the final code, in the full gate.Pixel parity
The tests pass1,187 of 1,204 tests passed, 0 failed, 17 skipped (bin/verify, seed required); the Linux Cable suite 118 of 120.
Durable by defaultRails' settings, and every write committed before it is answered. The last kill -9 runs (4, in round three) lost 0 acknowledged posts and duplicated 0. Nothing in the database or writer changed in round five, so the durability test was not repeated.Durability
Attacked, and fixedEvery round closed with an adversarial verifier or a skeptical review; what they found was fixed with a test that fails on the code before. Round five's three reader-protocol defects and a scratch leak are the latest.The first round's attacks
Memory has a boundCable keeps what a slow client has not read once, in a shared log, and the hub's total is bounded at 1 GiB; over it, the clients furthest behind are cut. A client that reads is never cut.
Size41.9 KLOC by upstream's rules, against 31.0 for Rust, 94.9 for C and 38.2 for the F# port it was forked from.The size table

The price

Rust accepts posts faster than it can send them and cuts the readers who cannot keep up; onCrack slows the posters and keeps everyone. Neither is wrong; they protect different things. Rails keeps everyone too, at 18.6 posts a second and about 3,259 MB.

cable_heavy: 1,000 clients, 64 closed-loop posters, medians of 3 rounds

What does not hold

  • Memory. onCrack's is 2.70× to 2.77× of Rust's in the Cable suite and about a gigabyte in cable_heavy.
  • Rust is faster in paced latency at 100 clients (3.3 against 5.2 ms) and ties on throughput at 2,000; the fan-out panel has the reps.
  • The speed claim has a range and no quiet repeat: the evidence for claim one.
  • No clean first-pass pixel gate (three harness faults, each passed on re-run) and a timing test in the Linux Cable suite that may still flake.

Not done here and not mine to do: publishing. The repository, its About section, Pages and the pull request are the operator's.

The iterations

What changed in each one

×

Every iteration of the chart, what changed in it, the headline each closed with as its own report wrote it, and the gate. The headlines are not comparable down the column: rounds one and two's early figures divide by the pinned Rust (ccece30) on this project's own suite; from round two's final run they divide by current Rust (f9dca47) and C (cd0cbe4) on upstream's harness, in sessions that differ in host noise.

What changed, iteration by iteration
IterationWhat changedHeadline at its closeGate
Port, the buildThe Rust workspace translated crate by crate to F# on ASP.NET Core and Falco: scaffold and plan; Ruby, RailsCompat, Routes, Assets; Db, RichText, Storage; Kit core, front server, Cable; the views; the app: boot, account controllers, the hot path, channels and integrations.The first baseline: 0.68×–0.79× Rust on the four reads at 16 connections, 1.02× on posts, 20–92 Rails.Ported vectors and tests per crate; the image boots under the parity candidate.
Port, the tuningThe parity loop, then five tuning units against Rust's profile: signed-cookie requests, identity bodies, Db row reads, rich text, plain-frame Cable fan-out. The last phase (Datastar) was dropped. Published as the F# port (fork point 0ae3436).phase7-final: 1.24×–1.33× Rust at 16 connections, with less CPU per request than Rust.The parity harness.
Round oneThe brief: same pixels, unhinged work per request. C0 instruments; C1 a versioned read cache (per-room and per-user counters bumped by temporary triggers, a page cache, authentication through the cache); C2 group commit (up to 64 writes, one commit) and a post broadcast in commit order; C3 Content-Length on gzipped answers; C4 Native AOT, shipped as an opt-in; four verifier findings fixed.3.84× Rust and 2.89× the port at 16 connections (2.06× at one, 4.54× at 64), a result in which every read was a cache hit.940 of 940 screenshots pixel-equal.
Round twoR2.0 made the benchmark honest (realistic workloads that write while they read); R2.1 Cable writes its own socket (probe and pong, one wake for both of a post's broadcasts); R2.2 posting work cut with Rails' durability kept; R2.3 a front-server fast path; R2.4 one connection; R2.5 memory and cold start. The verifier's seven findings were fixed, a critical one among them. It ended against upstream's own harness and current Rust, C and Rails.3.25× Rust, 2.37× C, 3.93× the port (normal), 3.64× and 2.36× on mixed reads, with the cached decision, which is not upstream's contract.940 of 940 round one's gate; a 252-screenshot targeted gate after the fixes.
Round threeR3.1 the full gate on the final code; R3.2 fresh authorization on every cache hit became the default (upstream's contract; the cached decision kept as an opt-in); R3.3 search ordered by message id as upstream's; R3.4 the WAL-restart stall traced to the VM's disk (default unchanged).Fresh: 2.59× Rust, 1.86× C, 3.82× the port (normal, two sessions pooled; the sessions alone 2.68× and 3.33×); mixed 3.31× and 2.06×; CPU per room page 2.72× Rust, 1.89× C.940 of 940.
Round fourR4.0 the one failing attack test was the test browser's cookie jar; R4.1 a raw epoll Cable client that measures the server (with a window, since a client that keeps up laps the rings); R4.2 gather writes (sendmsg); R4.3 the fresh check holds a read transaction; R4.4 WAL volume, measured, nothing shipped; R4.5 Cable reliability: a byte-bounded shared log, publish order across streams, a cut for a stall and not for slowness, a posting gate. The verifier's four defects were fixed.3.29× Rust, 2.40× C, 4.01× the port (one session); CPU per room page 3.25× Rust, 2.02× C; fan-out 1.59×, 1.24×, 1.16× and 0.94× Rust (the “ahead at every count” sentence withdrawn); PR #6 incomplete: onCrack the only app to keep all 1,000 clients in cable_heavy. Two defects left open: one message of 34,741 missing, and a memory gap.102 targeted screenshots.
Round fiveR5.1 the missing message traced to the server, a corrupted payload and not a lost frame; R5.2 the gather pinned only the last payload of each batch (a compiler had turned the recursion into a loop), and the hub's total now reaches every chunk and cuts the furthest behind; R5.3 the fan-out at 2,000 clients profiled (three quarters of the CPU in sendmsg), the hold and batch settings kept nothing. The verifier fixed three reader-protocol defects and a scratch leak. Then the final gates and runs.3.76× Rust, 2.40× C, 5.25× the port (normal), 3.76×, 2.26× and 6.78× on mixed reads, across sessions of 2.11× to 4.74×; CPU per room page 3.79× Rust, 2.93× C; fan-out 1.65×, 1.24×, 1.17× and 1.01× Rust; PR #6: 0 of 1,000 clients cut, every round; 41.9 KLOC.944 of 944; bin/verify 1,187 passed, 0 failed.

Beats worth telling: the benchmark was made honest twice (round two's writing workloads, round four's load generator that stopped being the limit), and each time onCrack's number moved down before it moved up; the round-one multiple was a result in which every read was a cache hit; the default stopped being the fast mode in round three (fresh authorization) and round four then bought the cost back; and the one correctness doubt that survived round four, a message that did not reach a client, was a compiler turning a recursion into a loop, found by reading the IL.

The climb

Every dot, and how to read the chart

×

Each line is the geometric mean of throughput over Rust's across the five benchmarked workloads (room page, messages page, sidebar, search, post a message) at 16 connections. Dots are spaced evenly in the order they ran, grouped under their iteration; the time under a dot is the clock. A dot that measured only some workloads carries the rest from the last kept run; its card greys them.

Read with care

  • Two denominators, both pinned Rust. The port's dots divide by the Rust measured in the session of its own tuning phase's start (or, for its first two, in the same run); onCrack's divide by the stored Rust medians of the port's final re-baseline (phase7-final), so onCrack's dots compare with each other. The fork dot is on both lines: the same session, read against its own Rust. The headline at the top of the page is current upstream, measured with upstream's harness.
  • Fresh and cached are two lines. A logged row says which; a row without the field is cached, which is every row of rounds one and two. Only the round three and round five images were measured in both modes. The dotted segment from round two's last dot to the first fresh dot is not a measurement: it joins the line to where the default changed.
  • Round three's dots were measured in round five. Round three logged no project-suite row of its own, so its final image (37c5988) was measured then, beside round five's, in both modes; the cached rows are third attempts, the first two having run while other projects loaded the host (the selection rule was fixed before the third). Round four's final image was never measured on this suite.
  • Most dots are provisional. A tier 2 dot is one rep of the workloads a change touches, on a build mounted into a container. The numbers that count are tier 3: a rebuilt image, three reps, all five workloads.
  • Rails is a floor, and C is missing. Rails is the port's stored baseline, at a few percent of Rust's throughput on this suite. C was never run on it; its figures are on upstream's harness, at the top of the page.

The rules

What onCrack may and may not do

×

From plans/oncrack.md: “Make the UI exactly the same, but go unhinged with Datastar, caching, or any other improvements we can do.” The port matched the Rust port's work per request and still beat it. onCrack drops that constraint, and nothing else.

  1. The UI is identical. Every parity screen's pixels match Rails' (the harness's screenshot layer, lean matrix, all seeds) and every interaction behaves the same for a person using it. Server HTML, the live DOM, network requests and Cable frames may differ.
  2. Correct, always. No stale reads after a write, no data from one user in another's response, no lost messages. Every cache states its invalidation rule and has tests that try to break it.
  3. Durability is a disclosed choice. Anything that weakens it is measured both ways, documented, and shipped only behind a setting whose default is Rails-equivalent durability.
  4. Scored separately. Same harness, same seed and pinned CPUs; every ratio against the Rust port and against the F# port, never presented as a like-for-like port result.
  5. Same discipline. Measure before and after, one change at a time, log every run to the climb chart, never manufacture a win.

Source: plans/oncrack.md.

Before onCrack

The F# port's climb

×

onCrack was forked from the F# port, a faithful translation of the Rust port that matched Rust's work per request. The port's Phase 7 tuning climbed from 0.76× to 1.32× of Rust; they are the dotted line of the hero chart, and onCrack forks from its final dot. They measured a different rule (the same work as Rust) against the Rust of the port's own sessions. The port itself is at github.com/ckluis/once-campfire-fSharp.
